len.name: len
len.summary: The length of a string, array, or map
len.doc: Returns the number of characters in a string, the number of elements in an array, or the number of entries in a map, like Python's `len`. For a string, characters are Unicode characters, not bytes, so `len("héllo")` is `5`.

gc_collect_cycles.name: gc_collect_cycles
gc_collect_cycles.doc: Runs the cycle collector immediately. Values are normally freed as soon as nothing refers to them, but objects that refer to each other in a cycle are only freed by the collector, which also runs automatically as possible cycles accumulate. See Memory management.

substr.name: substr

params.name: start
params.doc: The character position to start at, counting from `0`. A negative `start` counts from the end: `-1` is the last character.

params.name: length
params.doc: The maximum number of characters to return. A negative `length` leaves that many characters off the end. By default, everything to the end of the string.

substr.doc: Returns the characters of `text` starting at `start`, at most `length` of them. Positions and lengths count characters, not bytes, following PHP's rules for negative values.

strpos.name: strpos

params.name: offset
params.doc: The character position to start searching from. A negative offset counts from the end.

strpos.summary: Find the position of the first occurrence of a substring
strpos.doc: Returns the character position of the first occurrence of `needle` in `haystack`, at or after `offset`.

str_contains.name: str_contains
str_contains.summary: Determine if a string contains a substring
str_contains.doc: Checks whether `needle` occurs anywhere in `haystack`. The comparison is case-sensitive.

strcmp.name: strcmp
strcmp.doc: Returns -1 if `a` sorts before `b`, 0 if they're the same, and 1 if it sorts after, comparing by Unicode code point as `<` does, like PHP 8.2's `strcmp`. It's what a usort comparison returns to sort by a string.

str_starts_with.name: str_starts_with
str_starts_with.summary: Check if a string starts with a given substring
str_starts_with.doc: Checks whether `haystack` begins with `needle`. The comparison is case-sensitive.

str_ends_with.name: str_ends_with
str_ends_with.summary: Check if a string ends with a given substring
str_ends_with.doc: Checks whether `haystack` ends with `needle`. The comparison is case-sensitive.

str_replace.name: str_replace

params.name: replace
params.doc: The replacement for each occurrence of `search`.

params.name: subject
params.doc: The string to search and replace in.

str_replace.summary: Replace all occurrences of a substring
str_replace.doc: Returns `subject` with every occurrence of `search` replaced by `replace`, scanning from left to right. The argument order is PHP's: what to find, what to put, where.

htmlspecialchars.name: htmlspecialchars
htmlspecialchars.doc: Replaces `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, and `'` with HTML entities, as PHP's `htmlspecialchars` does by default, so text from users can be put in an HTML page or attribute without being read as markup.

sprintf.name: sprintf

params.name: values
params.doc: The values the placeholders use, in order.

sprintf.doc:
Returns `format` with each placeholder replaced by a formatted value, as PHP's `sprintf` does. A placeholder is written `%[argnum$][flags][width][.precision]specifier`; `%%` is a literal percent sign.


SpecifierFormats the value asExample

`s`A string; `.precision` is the maximum number of characters`sprintf("%.3s", "abcdef")` is `abc`
`d`An int`-42`
`u`An int as unsigned`sprintf("%u", -1)` is `18446744073709551615`
`f`, `F`A double with `.precision` decimals (default 6)`sprintf("%.2f", 3.14159)` is `3.14`
`e`, `E`Scientific notation with `.precision` decimals`sprintf("%.2e", 1234.5)` is `1.23e+3`
`g`, `G`Plain or scientific notation, whichever is shorter, with `.precision` significant digits`sprintf("%g", 0.00001234)` is `1.234e-5`
`x`, `X`An int in hexadecimal`sprintf("%x", 255)` is `ff`
`o`An int in octal`sprintf("%o", 8)` is `10`
`b`An int in binary`sprintf("%b", 5)` is `101`
`c`The character with that Unicode code point; width doesn't apply`sprintf("%c", 233)` is `é`



Before the widthEffect

`-`Left-justify within the width (the default is right)
`+`Show a `+` sign on positive numbers
`0`Pad with zeros instead of spaces; a sign stays in front
`'`charPad with any character, such as `'*` or `'·`


The width is the minimum number of characters. `argnum$` picks a value by position, from 1, so `%2$s` uses the second value and a value can be used more than once.

Values are converted as PHP converts them: `%d` truncates a double and reads the number at the start of a string (`"12abc"` is 12); `%f` reads a double from a string. With `%s`, bools are `1` and `0`, and doubles are written like to_string (`%g`, so `1e+20`), where PHP would write `1.0E+20`.

params.name: times
params.doc: How many times to repeat it. `0` gives an empty string.

strtoupper.name: strtoupper
strtoupper.doc: Returns `text` with its letters converted to uppercase. Latin (ASCII, Latin-1, and Latin Extended-A), Greek, and Cyrillic letters are converted; other characters are unchanged.

strtolower.name: strtolower
strtolower.doc: Returns `text` with its letters converted to lowercase. Latin, Greek, and Cyrillic letters are converted; other characters are unchanged.

ucfirst.name: ucfirst
ucfirst.summary: Make a string's first character uppercase
ucfirst.doc: Returns `text` with its first character converted to uppercase, using the same rules as `strtoupper`.

strrev.name: strrev
strrev.doc: Returns the characters of `text` in reverse order. Unlike PHP's byte-wise `strrev`, multi-byte UTF-8 characters stay intact.

trim.name: trim

params.name: characters
params.doc: The characters to strip. Each character in this string, including multi-byte ones, is stripped wherever it appears at either end. By default: space, tab, newline, and carriage return.

trim.summary: Strip characters from the beginning and end of a string
trim.doc: Returns `text` with leading and trailing characters from `characters` removed.

explode.name: explode

params.name: separator
params.doc: The string to split at. It must not be empty.

params.name: limit
params.doc: With a positive `limit`, at most that many pieces are returned, the last holding the rest of the string. With a negative `limit`, all pieces except the last `-limit` are returned. `0` counts as `1`.

explode.summary: Split a string by a separator
explode.doc: Splits `text` at each occurrence of `separator`, following PHP's rules.

implode.name: implode

params.name: separator
params.doc: The string to put between elements.

implode.summary: Join array elements with a string
implode.doc: Joins the strings in `pieces` with `separator` between each pair.

string_to_bytes.name: string_to_bytes
string_to_bytes.doc: Returns the UTF-8 encoding of `text`, one element per byte.

bytes_to_string.name: bytes_to_string
bytes_to_string.summary: Decode UTF-8 bytes into a string

preg_match.name: preg_match

params.name: offset
params.doc: The character to start searching from.

preg_match.summary: Find the first match of a pattern
preg_match.doc: Searches `subject` for `pattern` and returns the first match as a RegexMatch, with its text, position, and groups. Like PHP's `preg_match($pattern, $subject, $matches)`, but the match is returned rather than written into `$matches`.

preg_match_all.name: preg_match_all

params.name: offset
params.doc: The character to start searching from.

preg_match_all.summary: Find every match of a pattern
preg_match_all.doc: Returns every match of `pattern` in `subject`, in order, as RegexMatch objects. Matches don't overlap: each search starts where the previous match ended. This is PHP's `preg_match_all` with `PREG_SET_ORDER`: one object per match.

preg_test.name: preg_test
preg_test.doc: Returns whether `pattern` matches anywhere in `subject`. Use it where PHP code writes `if (preg_match(...))`.

preg_replace.name: preg_replace

params.name: replacement
params.doc: The text for each match, in which `$1` stands for the first group.

params.name: limit
params.doc: The most matches to replace; -1 for all.

preg_replace.doc: Returns `subject` with each match of `pattern` replaced by `replacement`. In the replacement, `$0` stands for the whole match, `$1` to `$99` for a group (`\1` and `${1}` work too), `${name}` for a named group, and `$$` for a dollar sign. A group that took no part in the match gives an empty string.

preg_replace_callback.name: preg_replace_callback

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each match; returns its replacement.

params.name: limit
params.doc: The most matches to replace; -1 for all.

preg_replace_callback.summary: Replace matches with what a function returns
preg_replace_callback.doc: Returns `subject` with each match of `pattern` replaced by what `callback` returns for it, for replacements that need computing.

preg_split.name: preg_split

params.name: pattern
params.doc: The pattern that separates the pieces.

params.name: limit
params.doc: Above 0, the most pieces to return, the last holding the rest; -1 for no limit.

params.name: skipEmpty
params.doc: Leave out empty pieces, as PHP's `PREG_SPLIT_NO_EMPTY`.

preg_split.summary: Split a string at matches of a pattern
preg_split.doc: Splits `subject` at each match of `pattern` and returns the pieces between them. Like `explode`, but the separator is a pattern.

preg_quote.name: preg_quote

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The pattern's delimiter, if it isn't one of the characters escaped anyway.

preg_quote.summary: Escape text for use in a pattern
preg_quote.doc: Returns `text` with a backslash before each character that has a meaning in a pattern (`. \ + * ? [ ^ ] $ ( ) { } = ! < > | : - #`) and before `delimiter`, so text from a user or a file can go inside a pattern and match only itself.

abs.name: abs
abs.doc: Returns `x` without its sign. It works on ints and on doubles and returns the same type: the compiler handles it for the types it's given.

min.name: min

params.name: values
params.doc: Two or more ints, or two or more doubles, or one array of them.

min.doc: Returns the smallest of its arguments, or of the elements of an array. It works on ints and on doubles and returns the same type: the compiler handles it for the types it's given.

max.name: max

params.name: values
params.doc: Two or more ints, or two or more doubles, or one array of them.

max.doc: Returns the largest of its arguments, or of the elements of an array. It works on ints and on doubles and returns the same type: the compiler handles it for the types it's given.

clamp.name: clamp
clamp.summary: Limit a value to a range
clamp.doc: Returns `x`, or `low` if `x` is below it, or `high` if it's above: `max(low, min(x, high))` in one call. It works on ints and on doubles and returns the same type: the compiler handles it for the types it's given. PHP has no `clamp`.

floor.name: floor
floor.doc: Returns the largest whole number not above `x`, as a double.

ceil.name: ceil
ceil.doc: Returns the smallest whole number not below `x`, as a double.

round.name: round

params.name: precision
params.doc: Decimal places; negative rounds to tens, hundreds, and so on.

round.summary: Round to a number of decimal places
round.doc: Returns `x` rounded to `precision` decimal places, with halves rounded away from zero, as PHP's `round` (see above).

number_format.name: number_format

params.name: decimals
params.doc: Decimal places; negative rounds before the point.

params.name: thousands
params.doc: Put between each group of three digits.

number_format.summary: Format a number with grouped thousands
number_format.doc: Returns `x` as text, rounded to `decimals` places as `round` rounds, with `thousands` between each group of three digits, as PHP's `number_format`. An int is written exactly, however large. A value that rounds to zero has no minus sign.

sqrt.name: sqrt
sqrt.doc: Returns the square root of `x`, or `NAN` for a negative number.

log.name: log

params.name: base
params.doc: The base; *e* (a natural logarithm) by default.

log.doc: Returns the logarithm of `x` to `base`. For bases 10 and 2, `log10` and `log2` are exact for powers of the base.

hypot.name: hypot
hypot.doc: Returns `sqrt(x * x + y * y)`, without overflowing for large values: the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin.

sin.name: sin
sin.doc: Returns the sine of `x`. `cos` and `tan` work the same way.

asin.name: asin
asin.doc: Returns the angle, in radians from -pi/2 to pi/2, whose sine is `x`; `NAN` outside -1 to 1.

acos.name: acos
acos.doc: Returns the angle, in radians from 0 to pi, whose cosine is `x`; `NAN` outside -1 to 1.

atan.name: atan
atan.doc: Returns the angle, in radians from -pi/2 to pi/2, whose tangent is `x`.

atan2.name: atan2
atan2.doc: Returns the angle of the point (x, y) from the positive x axis, in radians from -pi to pi, using the signs of both to find the quadrant.

is_nan.name: is_nan
is_nan.doc: Returns whether `x` is `NAN`, the result of operations such as `0.0 / 0.0` or `sqrt(-1.0)`. `NAN` isn't equal to anything, itself included, so `x == x` can't tell.

is_finite.name: is_finite
is_finite.doc: Returns whether `x` is neither infinite nor `NAN`.

is_infinite.name: is_infinite
is_infinite.doc: Returns whether `x` is `INF` or `-INF`, the result of dividing a nonzero double by zero, for example.

random_int.name: random_int
random_int.summary: A secure random int in a range
random_int.doc: Returns a random int from `min` to `max`, both included, each equally likely, from the operating system's secure random source, as PHP's `random_int`. It's suitable for tokens, codes, and passwords.

random_double.name: random_double
random_double.summary: A secure random double from 0 to 1
random_double.doc: Returns a random double from 0 up to, but not including, 1, from the operating system's secure random source, with every multiple of 2-53 in that range equally likely.

range.name: range

params.name: start
params.doc: The first value. Given alone, as `range(count)`, it's a count instead: see below.

params.name: end
params.doc: The last value, which is included if the steps land on it.

params.name: step
params.doc: The distance between values: positive, and for chars an int.

range.summary: A count from 0, or numbers or characters from start to end
range.doc:
`range(count)`, with one int, returns `0` up to `count - 1`: `range(3)` is `[0, 1, 2]`, and `range(0)` and a negative count give `[]`. It's the loop `for (i = 0; i < count; i++)` of other languages: `foreach (range(len(items)) as i)` goes through the indexes of `items`, and does nothing when it's empty. (PHP's `range` has no one-argument form.)

With two or three arguments, it returns the values from `start` to `end`, as PHP's `range` does:


- The result is `int[]` for ints, `double[]` if any argument is a double, and `char[]` for two chars, which count by Unicode code point (`range('a', 'e')`, `range('α', 'ε')`).

- The end is included: `range(1, 3)` is `[1, 2, 3]`. When `end` is less than `start`, the values count down: `range(3, 1)` is `[3, 2, 1]`. So `range(0, n - 1)` isn't empty when `n` is 0: it's `[0, -1]`. Use `range(n)`.

- For doubles, value i is `start + i * step`, stopping at `end`, so rounding can leave the end out: `range(0.0, 0.3, 0.1)` has three values.


In `foreach (range(...) as i)` over ints, no array is built: the loop just counts.

array_push.name: array_push

params.name: values
params.doc: One or more values to add, in order.

array_push.summary: Add values to the end of an array
array_push.doc: Appends the values to the end of the array. Appending is fast: the array keeps spare room, doubling it when it runs out.

array_pop.name: array_pop
array_pop.summary: Remove and return the last element
array_pop.doc: Removes the last element and returns it.

array_shift.name: array_shift
array_shift.summary: Remove and return the first element
array_shift.doc: Removes the first element and returns it. The other elements move down one place, so the old element 1 becomes element 0. This takes time proportional to the array's length.

array_unshift.name: array_unshift

params.name: values
params.doc: One or more values; they end up in the order given.

array_unshift.summary: Add values to the front of an array
array_unshift.doc: Inserts the values at the front of the array, moving the existing elements up. This takes time proportional to the array's length.

array_splice.name: array_splice

params.name: offset
params.doc: Where the range starts. A negative offset counts from the end.

params.name: length
params.doc: How many elements to remove; by default, all from `offset` to the end. A negative length leaves that many elements at the end.

params.name: replacement
params.doc: Elements to put in place of the removed ones; by default, none.

array_splice.summary: Remove or replace a range of elements
array_splice.doc: Removes `length` elements starting at `offset`, inserts the elements of `replacement` in their place, and moves the rest of the array to close or open the gap, as PHP's `array_splice` does. Offsets and lengths beyond the array's ends are clipped rather than errors. With a length of `0`, it only inserts.

sort.name: sort

params.name: array
params.doc: An array of ints, doubles, strings, chars, bytes, or bools.

sort.doc: Returns a new array with the elements in ascending order: numbers by value, strings and chars by their characters' Unicode code points (as PHP compares them, so `"Z"` comes before `"a"`, and accented letters after both), and `false` before `true`. Unlike PHP's `sort`, the array itself isn't changed. To sort anything else, or in another order, use usort.

rsort.name: rsort

params.name: array
params.doc: An array of ints, doubles, strings, chars, bytes, or bools.

rsort.summary: Sort an array in descending order
rsort.doc: Like sort, with the largest first.

usort.name: usort

params.name: array
params.doc: The array, of any element type.

params.name: compare
params.doc: Returns a negative int if its first argument goes first, a positive one if its second does, and 0 if they're equal.

usort.summary: Sort an array with a comparison function
usort.doc: Returns a new array with the elements in the order `compare` gives. The sort is stable: elements that compare equal keep their order, as in PHP 8. The comparison's parameters can leave out their types, which are the array's element type. Unlike PHP's `usort`, the array itself isn't changed.

in_array.name: in_array

params.name: value
params.doc: The value to look for, of the array's element type.

in_array.summary: Check whether an array has a value
in_array.doc: Returns whether any element equals `value`, as `==` compares them: numbers and strings by value, arrays and maps by their contents, and objects by identity. A value of another type is a compile error, so `in_array("1", [1, 2])` can't quietly match, as PHP's non-strict mode would.

array_search.name: array_search

params.name: value
params.doc: The value to look for, of the array's element type.

array_search.doc: Returns the index of the first element equal to `value`, as `==` compares them, or -1 if there is none. PHP's `array_search` returns `false` instead, which is easy to mistake for index 0.

array_slice.name: array_slice

params.name: offset
params.doc: Where to start; a negative offset counts from the end.

params.name: length
params.doc: How many elements to take; a negative length stops that many before the end. Without it, the slice runs to the end.

array_slice.doc: Returns a new array of the elements from `offset`, as PHP's `array_slice`. Offsets and lengths beyond the array are clamped to it, so the result can be empty but there's no error.

array_reverse.name: array_reverse
array_reverse.doc: Returns a new array with the elements in the opposite order.

array_unique.name: array_unique
array_unique.doc: Returns a new array with each value once, where it first appears, comparing as `==` does. Unlike PHP's `array_unique`, the result's indexes are 0, 1, 2, ..., as an array's always are.

array_sum.name: array_sum

params.name: array
params.doc: An array of ints or doubles.

array_sum.doc: Returns the sum of the elements, an int for an `int[]` (which wraps on overflow, as `+` does) and a double for a `double[]`. For an empty array, it's 0.

array_filter.name: array_filter

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each element; returns whether to keep it.

array_filter.doc: Returns a new array of the elements for which `callback` returns `true`, in order. Unlike PHP's `array_filter`, the result's indexes are 0, 1, 2, ..., as an array's always are. The callback can be an anonymous function, whose parameters can leave out their types (they come from the array's elements), a named function, or a function value.

array_map.name: array_map

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each element; returns its replacement, of any type.

array_map.doc: Returns a new array of what `callback` returns for each element, in order. The result's element type is the callback's return type, so it can differ from the array's. The callback can be an anonymous function, whose parameters can leave out their types (they come from the array's elements), a named function, or a function value.

array_reduce.name: array_reduce

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with the value so far and each element; returns the new value so far.

params.name: initial
params.doc: The value to start from, which is also the result for an empty array.

array_reduce.summary: Combine the elements into one value
array_reduce.doc: Calls `callback` with `initial` and the first element, then with its result and the second element, and so on, and returns the last result. The result's type is `initial`'s; an empty `[]` or `{}` takes the type the result is used as.

array_find.name: array_find

params.name: array
params.doc: An array of strings, arrays, maps, or objects.

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each element until it returns true.

array_find.summary: The first element a callback accepts
array_find.doc: Returns the first element for which `callback` returns `true`, or `null` if there is none, like PHP 8.4's `array_find`. The rest of the elements aren't looked at. Ints, doubles, bools, bytes, and chars can't be `null`, so for arrays of them, use array_find_index.

array_find_index.name: array_find_index

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each element until it returns true.

array_find_index.summary: The index of the first element a callback accepts
array_find_index.doc: Returns the index of the first element for which `callback` returns `true`, or -1 if there is none, like PHP 8.4's `array_find_key`. It works for arrays of any type.

array_any.name: array_any

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each element until it returns true.

array_any.summary: Whether a callback accepts any element
array_any.doc: Returns whether `callback` returns `true` for at least one element, like PHP 8.4's `array_any`, stopping at the first. For an empty array, it's `false`.

array_all.name: array_all

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each element until it returns false.

array_all.summary: Whether a callback accepts every element
array_all.doc: Returns whether `callback` returns `true` for every element, like PHP 8.4's `array_all`, stopping at the first that fails. For an empty array, it's `true`.

map_key_exists.name: map_key_exists

params.name: key
params.doc: The key to look for, of the map's key type.

map_key_exists.summary: Check whether a map has a key
map_key_exists.doc: Returns whether `map` has an entry for `key`. An entry whose value is `null` still counts.

map_keys.name: map_keys
map_keys.summary: The keys of a map, as an array
map_keys.doc: Returns a new array of the map's keys, in the order they were added.

map_values.name: map_values
map_values.summary: The values of a map, as an array
map_values.doc: Returns a new array of the map's values, in the order their keys were added. The array refers to the same arrays, maps, and objects as the map; it doesn't copy them.

in_map.name: in_map

params.name: value
params.doc: The value to look for, of the map's value type.

in_map.summary: Check whether a map has a value
in_map.doc: Returns whether any entry of `map` has `value`. Values compare as `==` compares them: numbers and bools by value, strings and chars by content, and arrays and maps by contents (the same elements in order, or the same keys and values in any order). Objects and functions compare by identity: the same instance, not an equal one.

map_merge.name: map_merge

params.name: maps
params.doc: Two or more maps of the same type.

map_merge.doc: Returns a new map with every entry of every map. For a key in more than one, the value from the last map wins, in the place the key first appeared, as with PHP's `array_merge` for string keys (and unlike it for int keys, which keep their values rather than being renumbered). The maps aren't changed.

map_diff_keys.name: map_diff_keys

params.name: map
params.doc: The map to take entries from.

params.name: other
params.doc: The map whose keys to leave out; its values can be of any type.

map_diff_keys.summary: The entries whose keys another map doesn't have
map_diff_keys.doc: Returns a new map with the entries of `map` whose key isn't in `other`, in `map`'s order, like PHP's `array_diff_key`. Only keys are compared, so the two maps need the same key type but not the same value type.

map_intersect_keys.name: map_intersect_keys

params.name: map
params.doc: The map to take entries from.

params.name: other
params.doc: The map whose keys to keep; its values can be of any type.

map_intersect_keys.summary: The entries whose keys another map has
map_intersect_keys.doc: Returns a new map with the entries of `map` whose key is also in `other`, in `map`'s order, with `map`'s values, like PHP's `array_intersect_key`. Only keys are compared, so the two maps need the same key type but not the same value type.

map_diff.name: map_diff

params.name: map
params.doc: The map to take entries from.

params.name: other
params.doc: A map of the same type.

map_diff.summary: The entries another map doesn't have
map_diff.doc: Returns a new map with the entries of `map` that `other` doesn't have: whose key isn't in `other`, or is with a different value. Like PHP's `array_diff_assoc`. Values compare as `==` compares them, as in in_map.

map_intersect.name: map_intersect

params.name: map
params.doc: The map to take entries from.

params.name: other
params.doc: A map of the same type.

map_intersect.summary: The entries another map has too
map_intersect.doc: Returns a new map with the entries of `map` that `other` also has, with the same key and an equal value. Like PHP's `array_intersect_assoc`. Values compare as `==` compares them.

map_flip.name: map_flip

params.name: map
params.doc: A map whose values can be keys: ints, doubles, bools, strings, or chars.

map_flip.doc: Returns a new map whose keys are `map`'s values and whose values are its keys, like PHP's `array_flip`. A value that appears more than once becomes one key, with the last key it had.

map_filter.name: map_filter

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each key and value; returns whether to keep the entry.

map_filter.doc: Returns a new map of the entries for which `callback` returns `true`, in the map's order, like PHP's `array_filter` with `ARRAY_FILTER_USE_BOTH`. The callback can be an anonymous function, whose parameters can leave out their types (they come from the map), a named function, or a function value.

map_map.name: map_map

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called with each value; returns its replacement, of any type.

map_map.summary: Transform each value, keeping the keys
map_map.doc: Returns a new map with the same keys, in the same order, and what `callback` returns for each value, like PHP's `array_map` on an associative array. The new values' type is the callback's return type. The callback can be an anonymous function, whose parameters can leave out their types (they come from the map), a named function, or a function value.

unset.name: unset

params.name: entry
params.doc: The entry to remove, written as an index: `unset(ages["ada"])`.

unset.summary: Remove an entry from a map
unset.doc: Removes the entry for the key, if there is one; removing a key that isn't there does nothing, as in PHP. The other entries keep their order. For arrays, use array_splice, which moves the later elements down.

file_get_contents.name: file_get_contents
file_get_contents.summary: Read an entire file into a string
file_get_contents.doc: Reads the whole file at `path` as text.

file_put_contents.name: file_put_contents

params.name: path
params.doc: The file to write. It's created if it doesn't exist.

params.name: append
params.doc: When `true`, add to the end of the file instead of replacing its contents.

file_put_contents.summary: Write a string to a file

file.name: file
file.summary: Read a file into an array of lines
file.doc: Reads the file at `path` and splits it into lines. Line endings (`\n` or `\r\n`) are removed, and a final line ending doesn't add an empty line.

file_exists.name: file_exists
file_exists.summary: Check whether a file or directory exists

is_file.name: is_file
is_file.summary: Check whether a path is a regular file
is_file.doc: Checks whether `path` exists and is a regular file.

is_dir.name: is_dir
is_dir.summary: Check whether a path is a directory
is_dir.doc: Checks whether `path` exists and is a directory.

scandir.name: scandir
scandir.summary: List the names in a directory
scandir.doc: Lists the files and directories inside `path`.

file_get_bytes.name: file_get_bytes
file_get_bytes.summary: Read an entire file as raw bytes
file_get_bytes.doc: Reads the file at `path` without interpreting it, so it works for any file, including images, archives, and text that isn't UTF-8.

file_put_bytes.name: file_put_bytes

params.name: path
params.doc: The file to write. It's created if it doesn't exist.

params.name: append
params.doc: When `true`, add to the end of the file instead of replacing it.

file_put_bytes.summary: Write raw bytes to a file
file_put_bytes.doc: Writes `data` to the file at `path` exactly as given.

basename.name: basename
basename.summary: The last part of a path
basename.doc: Gives the name at the end of `path`, ignoring trailing slashes. It works on the text alone and doesn't look at the disk.

dirname.name: dirname
dirname.summary: A path without its last part
dirname.doc: Gives the directory part of `path`: everything before the last part, ignoring trailing slashes, cleaned as `path_clean` does. It works on the text alone.

path_ext.name: path_ext
path_ext.doc: Gives the extension of the last part of `path`: from its last `.` to the end.

path_join.name: path_join

params.name: parts
params.doc: The parts, in order. Pass an array with `...parts`.

path_join.doc: Joins the parts with `/` and cleans the result as `path_clean` does. Empty parts are skipped. An absolute part doesn't start the path again: `path_join("a", "/b")` is `a/b`.

path_clean.name: path_clean
path_clean.doc: Gives the shortest path to the same place, by the text alone: one `/` between parts, no `.` parts, no trailing slash, and each `..` removed along with the part before it. At the root, `..` stays at the root; a relative path keeps the `..` parts it can't remove.

path_is_absolute.name: path_is_absolute
path_is_absolute.summary: Check whether a path starts at the root

path_rel.name: path_rel
path_rel.summary: The relative path from one path to another
path_rel.doc: Gives a relative path that leads from `base` to `target`, so that `path_join(base, path_rel(base, target))` is `path_clean(target)`. Only the text is compared.

realpath.name: realpath
realpath.summary: The absolute path, with links resolved
realpath.doc: Resolves `path` on the disk: makes it absolute from the current directory, and resolves `.`, `..`, and symbolic links.

mkdir.name: mkdir

params.name: recursive
params.doc: When `true`, also create the missing directories above it, and don't fail if it already exists.

mkdir.doc: Creates the directory `path`, which anyone can read and enter (as the system's umask allows).

rmdir.name: rmdir

params.name: recursive
params.doc: When `true`, remove everything in it first.

rmdir.doc: Removes the directory `path`. Without `recursive` it must be empty. With it, the files and directories inside are removed too; symbolic links inside are removed, not followed.

unlink.name: unlink
unlink.doc: Deletes the file (or symbolic link) at `path`. A program that still has the file open can go on using it.

rename.name: rename

params.name: from
params.doc: The file or directory to move.

rename.summary: Move or rename a file or directory
rename.doc: Moves `from` to `to` in one step, replacing a file already at `to`. Writing a new file and renaming it over the old one replaces a file so that readers never see it half written.

copy.name: copy
copy.doc: Copies the contents and permissions of the file `from` to `to`, replacing a file already there.

filesize.name: filesize
filesize.doc: Gives the size of the file at `path`.

filemtime.name: filemtime
filemtime.summary: When a file was last changed
filemtime.doc: Gives the time the contents of `path` last changed.

getcwd.name: getcwd
getcwd.doc: Gives the directory the program is running in. Relative paths start from it.

chdir.name: chdir
chdir.doc: Makes `path` the directory the program runs in, so relative paths start from there. It also changes the directory of programs started afterwards with `exec` and `shell` (unless they're given a `cwd`).

temp_dir.name: temp_dir
temp_dir.doc: Gives the directory for temporary files: the `TMPDIR` environment variable, or `/tmp` when it isn't set.

temp_file.name: temp_file

params.name: prefix
params.doc: The start of the file's name.

temp_file.doc: Creates a new, empty file in `temp_dir()`, named `prefix` followed by six random characters, that only the user running the program can read and write. The name is chosen so that it can't clash with an existing file.

glob.name: glob
glob.summary: Find paths that match a pattern
glob.doc: Finds the files and directories that match `pattern`: `*` matches any run of characters within one part of a path, `?` one character, and `[abc]` one of the characters listed (`[a-z]` one in a range). A name starting with `.` matches only a pattern part that starts with `.`.

csv_parse.name: csv_parse

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

csv_parse.doc: Reads every record of `text`, each as an array of its fields, like PHP's `str_getcsv` for a whole text, or Python's `csv.reader`.

csv_parse_maps.name: csv_parse_maps

params.name: text
params.doc: The CSV, with a header row.

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

csv_parse_maps.summary: Read CSV text by column name
csv_parse_maps.doc: Reads the first record as a header of column names, and each record after it as a map from those names to its fields.

csv_decode.name: csv_decode

params.name: text
params.doc: The CSV, with a header row.

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

csv_decode.doc: Reads each record after the header into a new object of the class the result is used as, as json_decode does for JSON: each public property is set from the column with its name, converted to the property's type. Columns without a property are ignored, and the columns can be in any order. Around ints, doubles, and bools, spaces are ignored; bools are `true`, `false`, `1`, `0`, `yes`, or `no`, in any case.

csv_encode.name: csv_encode

params.name: objects
params.doc: The objects, of a class whose public properties are ints, doubles, bools, or strings.

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

csv_encode.doc: Writes a header of the class's public property names, then a row for each object, with each property as `print` would write it (bools as `true` and `false`, and a null string as an empty field). What it writes, csv_decode reads back.

csv_format.name: csv_format

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

csv_format.doc: Writes each row as a line of CSV, quoting a field only when it holds the delimiter, a quote, or a line break.

csv_read.name: csv_read

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

csv_read.summary: Read a CSV file as rows
csv_read.doc: Reads the whole file, as csv_parse reads text. For files too large to read at once, use CsvReader.

csv_read_maps.name: csv_read_maps

params.name: path
params.doc: The file, with a header row.

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

csv_read_maps.summary: Read a CSV file by column name
csv_read_maps.doc: Reads the whole file, as csv_parse_maps reads text.

csv_write.name: csv_write

params.name: delimiter
params.doc: The character between fields: `","`, `";"` for files from Excel in many European locales, or `"\t"` for tab-separated values.

params.name: append
params.doc: Add to the end of the file instead of replacing it.

csv_write.summary: Write rows to a CSV file
csv_write.doc: Writes `rows` to the file as csv_format formats them, creating the file if it doesn't exist. For a row at a time, use CsvWriter.

time.name: time
time.doc: Returns the current time as a timestamp. A *timestamp* is an `int` counting seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.

microtime.name: microtime
microtime.doc: Returns the current time in seconds since the Unix epoch, with microseconds, like PHP's `microtime(true)`.

hrtime.name: hrtime
hrtime.doc: Returns nanoseconds from a monotonic clock. The value has no fixed starting point, so only the difference between two readings is meaningful, and it never jumps when the system clock is changed.

date.name: date

params.name: format
params.doc: The format, made of the format characters.

params.name: timestamp
params.doc: Defaults to the current time. The default value, the smallest int, stands for "now", because qiq defaults must be literals.

date.summary: Format a timestamp in the current timezone
date.doc: Formats `timestamp` as local time in the current timezone, using PHP's format letters. Characters that aren't format letters are copied unchanged.

gmdate.name: gmdate

params.name: format
params.doc: The format, made of the format characters.

params.name: timestamp
params.doc: Defaults to the current time. The default value, the smallest int, stands for "now", because qiq defaults must be literals.

gmdate.doc: Like `date`, but always formats the time in UTC: `e` prints `UTC`, `T` prints `GMT`, and offsets are zero.

mktime.name: mktime
mktime.summary: Build a timestamp from a local date and time
mktime.doc: Returns the timestamp of a date and time in the current timezone. Values outside their usual range roll over into the next field, as in PHP: month 13 is January of the next year, and day 0 is the last day of the previous month. The argument order is PHP's; named arguments make calls clearer.

gmmktime.name: gmmktime
gmmktime.summary: Build a timestamp from a UTC date and time
gmmktime.doc: Like `mktime`, but the date and time are in UTC. Out-of-range values roll over the same way.

checkdate.name: checkdate
checkdate.doc: Checks that the date exists in the Gregorian calendar, taking leap years into account.

strtotime.name: strtotime

params.name: text
params.doc: An ISO 8601 date, or date and time.

strtotime.doc:
Parses a date in one of these ISO 8601 forms:

- a date: `2026-11-19` (midnight)

- a date and time, separated by `T` or a space: `2026-11-19 14:30`, `2026-11-19T14:30:00`; fractions of a second (`14:30:00.250`) are accepted and dropped

- either of those followed by `Z` or an offset: `2026-11-19T14:30:00Z`, `+02:00`, `-0500`, `+05`


Without `Z` or an offset, the time is local, in the current timezone.

date_default_timezone_set.name: date_default_timezone_set

params.name: zone
params.doc: A zone name from the tz database, such as `"Europe/London"`, `"America/New_York"`, or `"UTC"`.

date_default_timezone_set.summary: Set the timezone for local times
date_default_timezone_set.doc: Sets the timezone used by `date`, `mktime`, and `strtotime` for the rest of the program. Without a call, the system timezone is used.

date_default_timezone_get.name: date_default_timezone_get
date_default_timezone_get.doc: Returns the zone set with `date_default_timezone_set`. Otherwise it returns the system's zone: the `TZ` environment variable if it's set, else the zone `/etc/localtime` links to, else `"UTC"`.

params.name: microseconds
params.doc: How long to pause; one second is `1000000`.

json_encode.name: json_encode

params.name: value
params.doc: The value to encode: any type.

params.name: pretty
params.doc: Whether to indent the output (4 spaces per level, one value per line), like PHP's `JSON_PRETTY_PRINT`.

json_encode.doc: Returns the JSON text for `value`. Objects are written with their public properties, in the order they're declared (inherited properties first); private and protected properties are left out. Maps are written in insertion order, as PHP writes arrays. A case of a backed enum is written as its value.

json_decode.name: json_decode
json_decode.summary: Convert JSON to a typed value
json_decode.doc:
Parses `text` and builds a value of the type the result is used as, checking that the JSON matches it:


- The type comes from where the call is used: `User user = json_decode(text);`, an assignment, a property, an argument, or a return value. Without one, such as in `print(json_decode(text))`, it's a compile error.

- For a class, the JSON object's keys are matched to public properties by name. Keys the class doesn't have are ignored, and properties the JSON doesn't mention keep their default (zero, `false`, or `null`). The constructor isn't called. The class, and every class reachable through its public properties, must be concrete, which the compiler checks.

- `null` is accepted wherever a string, char, array, map, or object is expected. If a key appears twice, the last value wins.

http_request.name: http_request

params.name: method
params.doc: The method, such as `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, or `HEAD`; any case.

params.name: body
params.doc: The request body, sent as is; `null` for none.

params.name: headers
params.doc: Headers to send, added to the defaults.

params.name: timeout
params.doc: Seconds to wait for each connect, read, and write.

http_request.doc: Sends the request, follows redirects, and returns the final Response. Set a `Content-Type` header to describe a body, such as `application/json`.

http_get.name: http_get

params.name: timeout
params.doc: Seconds to wait for each connect, read, and write.

http_get.doc: Same as `http_request("GET", url, null, headers, timeout)`.

http_post.name: http_post

params.name: timeout
params.doc: Seconds to wait for each connect, read, and write.

http_post.doc: Same as `http_request("POST", url, body, headers, timeout)`.

urlencode.name: urlencode
urlencode.summary: Percent-encode text for a query string
urlencode.doc: Encodes the text's UTF-8 bytes as `%XX`, except letters, digits, and `-_.`, and writes spaces as `+`, as PHP's `urlencode` does. Use it for query strings and form bodies; for path segments, use rawurlencode.

rawurlencode.name: rawurlencode
rawurlencode.summary: Percent-encode text for a URL path
rawurlencode.doc: Encodes the text's UTF-8 bytes as `%XX`, except letters, digits, and `-_.~` (RFC 3986), as PHP's `rawurlencode` does. Spaces become `%20`.

urldecode.name: urldecode
urldecode.doc: Decodes `%XX` sequences, and `+` as a space, as PHP's `urldecode` does. A `%` that isn't followed by two hex digits is kept as is.

rawurldecode.name: rawurldecode
rawurldecode.doc: Decodes `%XX` sequences like urldecode, but leaves `+` as is, as PHP's `rawurldecode` does. Use it for URL paths, where `+` is an ordinary character.

http_build_query.name: http_build_query
http_build_query.summary: Build a query string from a map
http_build_query.doc: Returns `name=value` pairs joined with `&`, with names and values encoded by urlencode, in the map's order, as PHP's `http_build_query` does for a flat array.

http_serve.name: http_serve

params.name: address
params.doc: Where to listen: `":8080"` for every network interface (IPv4 and IPv6), `"127.0.0.1:8080"` for this machine only, `"[::1]:8080"` for an IPv6 address, or `"unix:/run/app.sock"` for a Unix socket file, to sit behind a proxy such as nginx.

params.name: workers
params.doc: The number of worker processes; `0` means one per CPU. With `1`, the server runs in this process without forking.

params.name: trustProxy
params.doc: Whether the server is behind a proxy such as nginx. If so, `Request::remoteAddress` is the client address the proxy forwarded (the last entry of `X-Forwarded-For`, or `X-Real-IP`), and `Request::scheme` comes from `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Only set it when clients can't reach the server except through the proxy, because anyone else could send those headers.

http_serve.doc: Listens on the address, starts the workers, and serves requests until the program gets SIGINT (Ctrl-C) or SIGTERM. Each worker serves one connection at a time; see How the server works.

http_file_server.name: http_file_server
http_file_server.summary: A handler that serves files from a directory
http_file_server.doc: Returns a handler that serves the file at the request's path inside `directory`, with a `Content-Type` from its extension (see http_content_type). For a directory, it serves its `index.html`, or a listing of its files; a directory path without a trailing `/` is redirected to one. Only `GET` and `HEAD` are allowed (405 otherwise), and a path containing a `..` segment gets 404, so files outside the directory can't be reached. Files are read whole into memory.

http_strip_prefix.name: http_strip_prefix

params.name: prefix
params.doc: The start of the path to remove, such as `"/static"`.

params.name: handler
params.doc: The handler to call with the shorter path.

http_strip_prefix.summary: Remove a prefix from the path before calling a handler
http_strip_prefix.doc: Returns a handler that removes `prefix` from the request's `path` and `rawPath` and calls `handler`, like Go's `http.StripPrefix`. A request whose path doesn't start with the prefix gets 404.

http_log.name: http_log
http_log.doc: Returns a handler that calls `handler` and then writes a line to stderr in the style of `php -S`: the time, the client's address, the status, the method, the path, and how long the handler took. A handler of this shape that wraps another is often called *middleware*; write your own the same way.

http_content_type.name: http_content_type
http_content_type.summary: The Content-Type for a file name
http_content_type.doc: Looks up the file's extension, in any case, among common web types: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, text, images, fonts, audio, video, PDF, archives, and WebAssembly. Text types include `; charset=utf-8`.

md5.name: md5

params.name: text
params.doc: The text to hash, as its UTF-8 bytes.

md5.doc: Returns the MD5 digest of `text` as 32 lowercase hex digits, like PHP's `md5`. The same as `hash("md5", text)`.

sha1.name: sha1

params.name: text
params.doc: The text to hash, as its UTF-8 bytes.

sha1.doc: Returns the SHA-1 digest of `text` as 40 lowercase hex digits, like PHP's `sha1`. The same as `hash("sha1", text)`.

hash.name: hash

params.name: algorithm
params.doc: The algorithm: `"md5"`, `"sha1"`, `"sha224"`, `"sha256"`, `"sha384"`, or `"sha512"`, in any case.

params.name: text
params.doc: The text to hash, as its UTF-8 bytes.

hash.summary: Compute a string's digest with a chosen algorithm
hash.doc: Returns the digest of `text` as lowercase hex, like PHP's `hash`.

hash_hmac.name: hash_hmac

params.name: algorithm
params.doc: The algorithm: `"md5"`, `"sha1"`, `"sha224"`, `"sha256"`, `"sha384"`, or `"sha512"`, in any case.

hash_hmac.doc: Returns the HMAC of `text` with `key` as lowercase hex, like PHP's `hash_hmac`, with the arguments in the same order. An HMAC shows that a message came from someone who knows the key and wasn't changed on the way, which is how webhooks and many APIs sign requests.

hash_bytes.name: hash_bytes

params.name: algorithm
params.doc: The algorithm: `"md5"`, `"sha1"`, `"sha224"`, `"sha256"`, `"sha384"`, or `"sha512"`, in any case.

hash_bytes.summary: Compute the raw digest of bytes
hash_bytes.doc: Returns the digest of `data` as bytes, like PHP's `hash` with `binary` set. Use it for data that isn't text, such as a file read with `file_get_bytes`, and where a raw digest is needed; bin2hex turns it into hex.

bin2hex.name: bin2hex
bin2hex.doc: Returns `data` as lowercase hex, two digits per byte, like PHP's `bin2hex`.

base64_encode.name: base64_encode

params.name: text
params.doc: The text, encoded as its UTF-8 bytes.

base64_encode.doc: Returns `text` in base64 (RFC 4648), with the standard alphabet and `=` padding, like PHP's `base64_encode`.

base64_encode_bytes.name: base64_encode_bytes
base64_encode_bytes.doc: Returns `data` in base64, as `base64_encode` does for text. Use it for binary data such as images, keys, and digests.

base64_decode.name: base64_decode
base64_decode.doc: Returns the text that `text` encodes. The standard and the URL-safe alphabets are both accepted (`+` or `-`, `/` or `_`), whitespace and line breaks are skipped, and the `=` padding may be left out. The bytes it decodes to must be UTF-8 text.

base64_decode_bytes.name: base64_decode_bytes
base64_decode_bytes.doc: Returns the bytes that `text` encodes, accepting what `base64_decode` accepts. Use it for binary data, and for the parts of a JWT, which use the URL-safe alphabet without padding.

bcrypt_hash.name: bcrypt_hash

params.name: password
params.doc: The password, as its UTF-8 bytes: at most 72 bytes.

params.name: cost
params.doc: How much work hashing takes, as a power of two: 4 to 31. Each step doubles the time; 12 takes about a third of a second.

bcrypt_hash.summary: Hash a password for storing, with bcrypt
bcrypt_hash.doc: Returns a bcrypt hash of `password` with a new random salt, in the form PHP's `password_hash` makes: 60 characters starting `$2y$` and the cost, as in `$2y$12$`. The salt and cost are part of the hash, so store the hash and nothing else, and check a password against it with bcrypt_verify. Hashing the same password twice gives different hashes.

bcrypt_verify.name: bcrypt_verify

params.name: hash
params.doc: A hash from `bcrypt_hash`: a bcrypt hash starting `$2y$`, `$2b$`, or `$2a$`.

bcrypt_verify.summary: Check a password against a bcrypt hash
bcrypt_verify.doc: Returns whether `password` is the password `hash` was made from, like PHP's `password_verify`. It hashes `password` again with the hash's salt and cost, so it takes as long as `bcrypt_hash` did, and compares the results in a way that takes the same time however much of them matches.

argv.name: argv
argv.doc: Returns the command line as a new array: element 0 is the program, and the arguments follow, as with PHP's `$argv`, Python's `sys.argv`, and Go's `os.Args`. With `qiq run app.qiq a b`, the program is `app.qiq`; with an executable built by `qiq build`, it's the path the executable was started with.

exit.name: exit
exit.summary: End the program with an exit status
exit.doc: Flushes output and ends the program immediately with `status`, which the shell sees as `$?`. Without `exit`, a program exits with 0, or with 1 after an uncaught exception.

getenv.name: getenv
getenv.doc: Returns the value of the environment variable `name`, or `null` if it isn't set. An empty value is an empty string, not `null`.

setenv.name: setenv
setenv.doc: Sets the environment variable `name` to `value` for the rest of the program, replacing any value it had. Like PHP's `putenv("NAME=value")`, with the name and value apart. It affects what `getenv` returns and what the standard library reads from the environment: `TZ` sets the default time zone for `date` and DateTime (unless `date_default_timezone_set` chose one), `PGPASSWORD` and `MYSQL_PWD` are read when a Database opens without a password in its URL, and `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` when the first TLS connection is made.

unsetenv.name: unsetenv
unsetenv.doc: Removes the environment variable `name`, so `getenv` returns `null` for it. Removing one that isn't set does nothing.

getpid.name: getpid
getpid.doc: Returns the process ID of the running program, like PHP's `getmypid`. Each worker process of the HTTP server has its own, which makes it useful in log lines; it's also a simple way to make a name unique on the machine, such as a temporary file's.

exec.name: exec

params.name: command
params.doc: The program followed by its arguments, such as `["git", "status"]`. The program is looked up on `PATH` unless it contains a `/`.

params.name: input
params.doc: Text written to the command's standard input. Without it, the command's standard input is empty.

params.name: cwd
params.doc: The directory the command runs in; the program's own by default.

params.name: env
params.doc: Environment variables to add or replace for the command. It also gets the program's other variables.

params.name: timeout
params.doc: Seconds the command may run before it's killed; 0 for no limit.

exec.summary: Run a program and wait for it
exec.doc: Runs `command`, waits for it to finish, and returns a ProcessResult with its exit status and everything it wrote to standard output and standard error. No shell is involved: each element of `command` reaches the program as one argument, exactly as given, so spaces, quotes, `$`, and `;` need no escaping and can't be used to inject another command. Use shell for pipes and redirects.

shell.name: shell

params.name: command
params.doc: A shell command line, such as `ls *.qiq | wc -l`.

params.name: input
params.doc: Text written to the command's standard input.

params.name: cwd
params.doc: The directory the command runs in.

params.name: env
params.doc: Environment variables to add or replace.

params.name: timeout
params.doc: Seconds before the command is killed; 0 for no limit.

shell.summary: Run a command with the system shell
shell.doc: Runs `command` with `/bin/sh -c`, for pipes, redirects, wildcards, `&&`, and variables, and returns a ProcessResult. It's `exec(["/bin/sh", "-c", command], ...)`, with the same settings and errors.

to_int.name: to_int
to_int.summary: Convert a value to an int
to_int.doc: Converts `value` to an `int`: a `byte` widens; `true` is `1` and `false` is `0`; a `double` is truncated toward zero; a `string` must be a whole int such as `"-42"` (an optional sign, then digits, with no spaces).

to_double.name: to_double
to_double.summary: Convert a value to a double
to_double.doc: Converts `value` to a `double`. A `string` must be a whole number such as `"2.5"`, `"-3"`, or `"1e5"`, with no leading spaces.

to_byte.name: to_byte

params.name: value
params.doc: The int to convert; it must be between 0 and 255.

to_byte.summary: Convert an int to a byte

to_string.name: to_string
to_string.summary: Convert a value to a string
to_string.doc: Converts `value` to text: ints and bytes in decimal, doubles formatted like `print` (`%g`), booleans as `true` or `false`, and a `char` as a one-character string.

print.name: print

params.name: values
params.doc: Zero or more values of any type except `void`.

print.doc: Writes its arguments on one line, separated by single spaces, followed by a newline. `print` is a statement built into the language, so it can't be passed around or redeclared.

println.name: println

params.name: values
params.doc: Zero or more values of any type except `void`.

println.summary: Write values to standard output, one per line
println.doc: Writes each of its arguments as print writes it, each on its own line. With one value or none, it's the same as `print`. Like `print`, it's a statement built into the language.

methods.name: getFile
methods.doc: The source file the exception was thrown in, or "" if unknown.

methods.name: getLine
methods.doc: The line it was thrown on, or 0 if unknown.

RuntimeException.name: RuntimeException
RuntimeException.doc: Errors that can only be detected while the program runs.

NetworkException.name: NetworkException
NetworkException.doc: A network connection failed: the host couldn't be found, refused the connection, timed out, or failed the TLS certificate check.

DatabaseException.name: DatabaseException
DatabaseException.doc: A database couldn't be opened, or rejected a statement: an SQL syntax error, a broken constraint, a missing table, or the wrong number of values for the placeholders (std/sql). getSqlState() is the standard five-character SQLSTATE ("42P01"; "HY000" for a general error) and getCode() the database's own error number (SQLite's extended result code, MySQL's error number; 0 for PostgreSQL, which has none).

ConstraintViolationException.name: ConstraintViolationException
ConstraintViolationException.doc: A statement broke a constraint (SQLSTATE class 23): NOT NULL, CHECK, a foreign key, or a unique key.

UniqueViolationException.name: UniqueViolationException
UniqueViolationException.doc: A row would duplicate another's value in a unique key or primary key.

ProcessException.name: ProcessException
ProcessException.doc: A map lookup used a key that is not in the map. A command couldn't be run (std/os exec and shell): it wasn't found, isn't executable, the working directory doesn't exist, or it ran past its timeout. A command that runs and exits with an error status doesn't throw; check ProcessResult's exitCode.

OutOfRangeException.name: OutOfRangeException
OutOfRangeException.doc: An array index is below 0 or not less than the array's length.

InvalidUtf8Exception.name: InvalidUtf8Exception
InvalidUtf8Exception.doc: A string is not valid UTF-8.

ArithmeticException.name: ArithmeticException
ArithmeticException.doc: An arithmetic operation has no result, such as a negative int exponent.

DivisionByZeroException.name: DivisionByZeroException
DivisionByZeroException.doc: `/` or `%` on ints with a zero right-hand side.

InvalidArgumentException.name: InvalidArgumentException
InvalidArgumentException.doc: A function was given an argument it cannot accept.

JsonException.name: JsonException
JsonException.doc: json_decode was given text that isn't JSON or doesn't match the type it decodes into, or json_encode was given a value JSON can't represent.

HttpException.name: HttpException
HttpException.doc: An HTTP request got an error status (from Response::raiseForStatus, with the status as its code) or was redirected too many times.

RegexException.name: RegexException
RegexException.doc: A regular expression (std/regex) is malformed, or needs too much backtracking on the text it's matched against.

CsvException.name: CsvException
CsvException.doc: CSV (std/csv) is malformed, such as a quoted field that's never closed, or doesn't fit what it's read into: a missing column, or a value that isn't a number where one is needed. The message names the line.

File.name: File
File.doc: A file opened for reading or writing a piece at a time, so large files don't have to fit in memory. Writes are buffered; close() (or the program ending) flushes them. Errors throw the same exceptions as the functions above, and using a file after close() throws IOException.

methods.name: open
methods.doc: Opens `path`. Modes: "r" read, "w" write (emptying the file first), "a" append, "x" create a new file (throws IOException if it exists); add "+" to also allow the other direction, e.g. "r+".

methods.name: readLine
methods.doc: The next line without its line ending ("\n" or "\r\n"), or null at the end of the file. Throws InvalidUtf8Exception if the line isn't UTF-8.

methods.name: read
methods.doc: Up to `length` bytes; fewer only at the end of the file, and an empty array after it.

methods.name: eof
methods.doc: Whether there is nothing left to read.

methods.name: flush
methods.doc: Writes buffered data to the file now.

methods.name: close
methods.doc: Flushes and closes the file. Closing twice does nothing. Closing stdin, stdout, or stderr only flushes them.

Duration.name: Duration
Duration.doc: A length of time, precise to the microsecond: what DateTime's until and since give, and what add and sub take. A day here is 24 hours; use DateTime's addDays for calendar days.

methods.name: totalDays
methods.doc: The length in whole units, rounded toward zero: 90 minutes is 1 hour.

DateTime.name: DateTime
DateTime.doc: An instant in time, shown in a time zone: like PHP's DateTimeImmutable, a DateTime never changes, and the methods that change something give a new one. Precise to the microsecond.

methods.name: now
methods.doc: The current time, in `zone` (or the default zone).

methods.name: of
methods.doc: A date and time on `zone`'s clock. Throws InvalidArgumentException for fields that don't make a date or time, such as April 31.

methods.name: fromTimestamp
methods.doc: The instant `seconds` after 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC (a Unix timestamp).

methods.name: fromTimestampMicros
methods.doc: The instant `microseconds` after 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.

methods.name: parse
methods.doc: Reads a date and time. Without a format: ISO 8601 and what databases write, such as "2026-11-22", "2026-11-22 10:30:00", or "2026-11-22T10:30:00.125+01:00". With one: PHP's createFromFormat letters, as in parse("22/11/2026 10:30", "d/m/Y H:i"). A time with an offset or zone of its own is in it; others are in `zone` (or the default zone). Throws InvalidArgumentException when it can't.

methods.name: dayOfWeek
methods.doc: 1 for Monday to 7 for Sunday, as ISO 8601 numbers them.

methods.name: dayOfYear
methods.doc: 1 for January 1.

methods.name: timestamp
methods.doc: Seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC (a Unix timestamp), rounded down.

methods.name: timestampMicros
methods.doc: Microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.

methods.name: zone
methods.doc: The zone's name: "Europe/London", "UTC", or "+05:30".

methods.name: offset
methods.doc: The zone's offset from UTC at this instant, in seconds: 3600 for +01:00.

methods.name: withZone
methods.doc: The same instant on another zone's clock.

methods.name: withDate
methods.doc: Another date at the same time of day.

methods.name: withTime
methods.doc: Another time of day on the same date.

methods.name: addYears
methods.doc: Calendar steps keep the time on the clock, across daylight saving changes too: a day later is the same time tomorrow, even when that's 23 or 25 hours away. A month or year later on a day the month doesn't have is its last day: January 31 plus a month is February 28 (or 29). Negative numbers go back.

methods.name: addHours
methods.doc: Steps of elapsed time: exactly that long later, whatever the clock says.

methods.name: startOfDay
methods.doc: 00:00:00 on this date (or the first time the day has, where midnight is skipped by a daylight saving change).

methods.name: isBefore
methods.doc: Comparisons are of instants, whatever the zones: 10:00 in London and 11:00 in Paris on the same winter day are equal.

methods.name: compareTo
methods.doc: -1, 0, or 1, as this is before, at, or after `other`.

methods.name: until
methods.doc: The time from this to `other`: negative when `other` is earlier.

methods.name: since
methods.doc: The time from `other` to this.

methods.name: format
methods.doc: With date()'s letters, as in format("D j M Y, H:i T"): also u for the microseconds, v for the milliseconds, and e for the zone's name.

ProcessResult.name: ProcessResult
ProcessResult.doc: What a command run by exec or shell did: its exit status and everything it wrote to standard output and standard error.

properties.name: exitCode
properties.doc: The exit status: 0 for success, 1 to 255 for failure, and 128 plus the signal's number if a signal ended the command.

properties.name: stdout
properties.doc: Everything the command wrote to standard output.

properties.name: stderr
properties.doc: Everything the command wrote to standard error.

methods.name: ok
methods.doc: Whether the command succeeded (exited with status 0).

methods.name: check
methods.doc: Throws ProcessException, with the exit status as its code and the error output in its message, unless the command succeeded. Returns the result, so `exec(...)->check()->stdout` reads the output of a command that must succeed.

Socket.name: Socket
Socket.doc: A connection to a server. Every connect, read, and write waits at most `timeout` seconds. With `tls`, the connection is encrypted and the server's certificate is checked against the system's CA certificates (or SSL_CERT_FILE). Failures throw NetworkException. Freeing a Socket doesn't close it; call close().

methods.name: readLine
methods.doc: The next line without "\n" or "\r\n", or null when the server has closed the connection. Bytes that aren't valid UTF-8 become U+FFFD.

methods.name: read
methods.doc: Up to `length` bytes, as soon as any arrive; an empty array once the server has closed the connection.

methods.name: readExactly
methods.doc: Exactly `length` bytes; throws NetworkException if the connection closes first.

methods.name: readAll
methods.doc: Everything until the server closes the connection.

methods.name: close
methods.doc: Closes the connection. Closing twice does nothing.

Url.name: Url
Url.doc: A URL, as RFC 3986 defines it: like Go's net/url URL, but immutable, as DateTime is: the methods that change something give a new Url.  Url search = Url::parse("https://api.example.com/v1/")->resolve("search")->withQuery("q", "café"); print(search); // https://api.example.com/v1/search?q=caf%C3%A9  The parts it returns are unescaped (path(), query(name), ...), except rawPath() and rawQuery(); the ones it's given are escaped as each part needs. Printing a Url, or to_string, gives it in full.

methods.name: parse
methods.doc: Reads a URL, absolute ("https://example.com/a?b=c#d") or relative ("../a", "?page=2"). Characters that should have been escaped, such as a space, are accepted and escaped. Throws InvalidArgumentException for one that can't be read: a bad %-escape, a port that isn't a number from 0 to 65535, or a host with characters a host can't have.

methods.name: scheme
methods.doc: The scheme, in lower case ("https"), or null for a relative URL.

methods.name: user
methods.doc: The user and password before the host, or null.

methods.name: host
methods.doc: The host without brackets ("example.com", "::1"), or null without one; "" for an empty one, as in file:///tmp/a.

methods.name: port
methods.doc: The port, or 0 when the URL doesn't give one.

methods.name: path
methods.doc: The path, unescaped: "/a b/c" for /a%20b/c.

methods.name: rawPath
methods.doc: The path as the URL writes it, escaped.

methods.name: rawQuery
methods.doc: What follows "?", escaped, or null when there's no "?".

methods.name: fragment
methods.doc: What follows "#", unescaped, or null when there's no "#".

methods.name: isAbsolute
methods.doc: Whether it has a scheme, so it stands on its own.

methods.name: query
methods.doc: The first value of the query parameter `name`, unescaped ("+" is a space), or null when there's none. "?flag" gives "" for flag.

methods.name: queryAll
methods.doc: Every value of the query parameter `name`, in order: ["a", "b"] for ?tag=a&tag=b.

methods.name: queryNames
methods.doc: The query parameters' names, each once, in the order they first come.

methods.name: withQuery
methods.doc: With the query parameter `name` set to `value` (escaped), in the place of its first value, without its others; at the end when it's new.

methods.name: withAddedQuery
methods.doc: With another value for `name` at the end: ?tag=a then ?tag=a&tag=b.

methods.name: withoutQuery
methods.doc: Without the query parameter `name` (none of its values).

methods.name: withRawQuery
methods.doc: With the whole query replaced by `raw` (written as it goes after "?", escaped), or no query for null.

methods.name: withScheme
methods.doc: With another scheme ("https"), or none for null.

methods.name: withUser
methods.doc: With another user and password (not escaped), or none for null.

methods.name: withHost
methods.doc: With another host: a name, an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 one (without brackets). null removes the host, with the user and port.

methods.name: withPort
methods.doc: With another port, or none for 0.

methods.name: withPath
methods.doc: With another path (unescaped: "/a b" becomes /a%20b).

methods.name: withFragment
methods.doc: With another fragment (unescaped), or none for null.

methods.name: resolve
methods.doc: `reference` resolved against this URL, as a browser resolves a link on this page (RFC 3986, section 5.2): "/b" keeps the scheme and host, "c" replaces the last segment of the path, "../c" goes up one, "?x" keeps the path, and an absolute URL is itself.

methods.name: equals
methods.doc: Whether the two are written the same way.

Response.name: Response
Response.doc: The response to an HTTP request.

properties.name: status
properties.doc: The status code, such as 200, and its reason phrase, such as "OK".

properties.name: headers
properties.doc: Header names in lowercase; a header sent more than once has its values joined with ", ".

properties.name: url
properties.doc: The URL that answered, after any redirects.

methods.name: text
methods.doc: The body as text. Throws InvalidUtf8Exception if it isn't UTF-8.

methods.name: header
methods.doc: A header's value, by name in any case, or null if it wasn't sent.

methods.name: ok
methods.doc: Whether the status is below 400, as in requests.

methods.name: raiseForStatus
methods.doc: Throws HttpException, with the status as its code, for a 4xx or 5xx status.

Request.name: Request
Request.doc: An HTTP request received by the server.

properties.name: rawPath
properties.doc: The path as the client sent it: "/files/a%20b.txt".

properties.name: rawQuery
properties.doc: What follows "?" in the URL, or "".

properties.name: scheme
properties.doc: "http", or "https" when a trusted proxy says the client used HTTPS (see http_serve's trustProxy).

properties.name: headers
properties.doc: Header names in lower case. Repeated headers are joined with ", ".

properties.name: remoteAddress
properties.doc: "address:port" of the client; "unix" for a client of a Unix socket. With http_serve's trustProxy, the address a proxy such as nginx forwarded, without a port.

properties.name: params
properties.doc: The path's wildcards, set by Router.

methods.name: text
methods.doc: The body as text; throws InvalidUtf8Exception if it isn't UTF-8.

methods.name: url
methods.doc: A header's value (the name in any case), or null. The URL the client asked for: the scheme (see trustProxy in http_serve), the Host header, the path, and the query.

methods.name: query
methods.doc: A query string field ("?page=2"), or null.

methods.name: form
methods.doc: A field of a form posted as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, then of the query string, or null.

methods.name: pathValue
methods.doc: The value of a wildcard in the Router pattern that matched, such as "id" in "/items/{id}", or null.

ResponseWriter.name: ResponseWriter
ResponseWriter.doc: Builds the response to a request. The status and headers can be changed until the handler returns; the body is sent with a Content-Length.

methods.name: status
methods.doc: Sets the status code (200 by default).

methods.name: header
methods.doc: Sets a header, replacing any with the same name in any case.

methods.name: getHeader
methods.doc: A header set so far (the name in any case), or null.

methods.name: write
methods.doc: Appends text to the body.

methods.name: redirect
methods.doc: Replies with a redirect to `url` (302 Found unless `code` says otherwise).

methods.name: error
methods.doc: Replies with `code` and its reason as plain text, like Go's http.Error: w->error(404) sends "404 Not Found".

methods.name: bytes
methods.doc: The body written so far.

Router.name: Router
Router.doc: Sends each request to the handler whose pattern matches it best, like Go's ServeMux. A pattern is "[METHOD ]/path":  "/about"            only /about "/static/"          /static/ and everything below it "/"                 everything (what nothing else matches) "/items/{id}"       /items/7, with r->pathValue("id") == "7" "/files/{path...}"  /files/a/b.txt, with path "a/b.txt" "/{$}"              only / itself "POST /items"       only POST requests; GET patterns also match HEAD  When several patterns match, the most specific wins: at the first segment where they differ, a fixed name beats {name}, which beats {name...} or a trailing "/"; then a longer pattern, then one with a method. A path that matches only with another method gets 405 Method Not Allowed; one that matches nothing, 404 Not Found. A path that matches only a "/dir/" pattern without its final slash is redirected to it.

methods.name: notFound
methods.doc: Sets the handler for paths that match no pattern (by default, a plain 404 Not Found).

methods.name: serve
methods.doc: Handles a request: finds the best route and calls its handler.

methods.name: handler
methods.doc: The router as a handler, for http_serve and the http_* wrappers.

Row.name: Row
Row.doc: One row of a query's result. Read a column by name with the getter for its type; a getter throws DatabaseException when the column doesn't exist or holds another type, so a mistake shows up where it is.

methods.name: columns
methods.doc: The column names, in the order the query gives them.

methods.name: has
methods.doc: Whether the result has a column named `column`.

methods.name: isNull
methods.doc: Whether the column is NULL.

methods.name: getInt
methods.doc: An INTEGER column. Throws when it's NULL or holds another type.

methods.name: getIntOr
methods.doc: An INTEGER column, or `fallback` when it's NULL.

methods.name: getDouble
methods.doc: A REAL column, or an INTEGER one as a double (as from AVG or SUM), or a PostgreSQL numeric.

methods.name: getDoubleOr
methods.doc: A REAL or INTEGER column, or `fallback` when it's NULL.

methods.name: getBool
methods.doc: An INTEGER column holding 0 or 1, as SQLite stores booleans.

methods.name: getBoolOr
methods.doc: A column holding 0 or 1, or `fallback` when it's NULL.

methods.name: getIntOrNull
methods.doc: An INTEGER column, or null when it's NULL.

methods.name: getDoubleOrNull
methods.doc: A REAL or INTEGER column, or null when it's NULL.

methods.name: getBoolOrNull
methods.doc: A column holding 0 or 1, or null when it's NULL.

methods.name: getString
methods.doc: A TEXT column (or a PostgreSQL numeric, as its exact text), or null when it's NULL (so `?? ""` gives a default). Text that isn't valid UTF-8 can only be read with getBytes.

methods.name: getBytes
methods.doc: A BLOB column, or null when it's NULL. Also reads TEXT that isn't valid UTF-8.

methods.name: getDateTime
methods.doc: A date and time column as a DateTime, or null when it's NULL: text such as a PostgreSQL timestamptz or a MySQL DATETIME (see DateTime::parse; a time without an offset is in `zone`, or the default zone), or an INTEGER Unix timestamp.

methods.name: toMap
methods.doc: The row as text, for printing and debugging: each column's value written as print writes it, NULL as null, and bytes as "(N bytes)".

Cursor.name: Cursor
Cursor.doc: The rows of a query, read a batch at a time rather than all at once, for results too big to hold in memory. From Database::cursor.  Cursor rows = db->cursor("select * from events where day = ?", day); Row row = rows->next(); while (row != null) { ... row = rows->next(); }  A cursor closes itself after its last row; close() stops early. With PostgreSQL and MySQL, the rows come from the connection as they're read, so the database can't run another statement until they've all been read or the cursor is closed (doing so throws DatabaseException).

methods.name: next
methods.doc: The next row, or null after the last.

methods.name: fetch
methods.doc: Up to `count` more rows: fewer only at the end, and none after it.

methods.name: close
methods.doc: Stops reading: the rest of the rows are skipped. Closing twice, or after the last row, does nothing.

methods.name: nextAs
methods.doc: The next row read into an object of the class the result is used as, as in `Event event = rows->nextAs();`, or null after the last.

methods.name: fetchAs
methods.doc: Up to `count` more rows read into objects of the class the result is used as, as in `Event[] batch = rows->fetchAs(500);`.

methods.name: open
methods.doc: Opens a database: "sqlite:path/to/file.db" (created if it doesn't exist), "sqlite::memory:" for one that lives in memory until it's closed, "postgres://user:password@host:5432/database", or "mysql://user:password@host:3306/database" (for MariaDB too; options after ?: sslmode=disable|require, connect_timeout=seconds). SQLite's URI names work too, such as "sqlite:file:data.db?mode=ro" to open read-only. A SQLite statement waits up to 5 seconds for another process's lock before throwing.

methods.name: execute
methods.doc: Runs one statement, such as an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or CREATE TABLE, with values for its placeholders. Returns how many rows it inserted, changed, or deleted.

methods.name: query
methods.doc: Runs a query with values for its placeholders and returns its rows.

methods.name: queryOne
methods.doc: The first row of a query, or null when there is none. The rest of the rows aren't read.

methods.name: cursor
methods.doc: Runs a query with values for its placeholders and returns a Cursor that reads its rows a batch at a time.

methods.name: executeScript
methods.doc: Runs several statements separated by semicolons, such as a schema; they can't have placeholders.

methods.name: lastInsertId
methods.doc: The rowid (the INTEGER PRIMARY KEY) of the last row inserted.

methods.name: begin
methods.doc: Transactions: changes made after begin() are saved together by commit(), or all undone by rollback(). Without one, each statement is saved on its own.

methods.name: inTransaction
methods.doc: Whether a transaction is open.

methods.name: transaction
methods.doc: Runs `body` in a transaction: commits when it returns, or rolls back and rethrows when it throws. Inside another transaction, it uses a savepoint instead: when `body` throws, only its own changes are rolled back, and the outer transaction carries on (or not) as its code decides; when it returns, its changes become part of the outer one.

methods.name: close
methods.doc: Closes the connection. Closing twice does nothing; using the database afterwards throws DatabaseException.

methods.name: queryAs
methods.doc: Runs a query and reads each row into an object of the class the result is used as, as in `User[] users = db->queryAs(sql, ...);`: through its constructor, by parameter name, or its public properties.

methods.name: queryOneAs
methods.doc: The first row of a query read into an object of the class the result is used as, as in `User user = db->queryOneAs(sql, ...);`, or null when there is none.

RegexMatch.name: RegexMatch
RegexMatch.doc: A match of a regular expression: the text it matched, where, and its groups.

properties.name: start
properties.doc: The positions of its first character and of the character after its last, so `end - start` is its length.

properties.name: groups
properties.doc: The whole match (element 0), then each group, in the order their opening parentheses appear. A group that took no part in the match, such as an unused alternative, is null.

methods.name: group
methods.doc: A group by number: 0 for the whole match, 1 for the first group. Null if the group took no part in the match. Throws OutOfRangeException if the pattern has no such group.

methods.name: named
methods.doc: A named group, written (?<name>...), or null if it took no part in the match. Throws InvalidArgumentException if the pattern has no group with that name.

methods.name: groupStart
methods.doc: Where a group starts and ends, by number, or -1 if it took no part in the match.

methods.name: namedGroups
methods.doc: The names of the named groups, each with its value (null for one that took no part in the match).

T.name: T
T.doc: The test being run, for its assertions.

methods.name: name
methods.doc: The test's function name, such as "test_add".

methods.name: equal
methods.doc: Fails unless `actual` equals `expected` (as == compares them). Either order works, but the message reads best with the value under test first: "expected 5, found 4".

methods.name: notEqual
methods.doc: Fails if `actual` equals `unexpected`.

methods.name: isTrue
methods.doc: Fails unless `condition` is true; `message`, if given, says what was expected.

methods.name: isFalse
methods.doc: Fails unless `condition` is false.

methods.name: near
methods.doc: Fails unless `actual` is within `tolerance` of `expected`, for doubles that arithmetic leaves slightly off: t->near(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3).

methods.name: throws
methods.doc: Fails unless calling `body` throws an exception of class `exception` (its own class, by name), or any exception for "Exception".

methods.name: fail
methods.doc: Fails the test with `message`.

methods.name: skip
methods.doc: Stops the test, which counts as skipped rather than failed.

methods.name: log
methods.doc: Notes `message`, shown if the test fails, or with qiq test -v.

CsvReader.name: CsvReader
CsvReader.doc: Reads a CSV file a record at a time, for files too large to read at once.

methods.name: open
methods.doc: Opens the CSV file at `path`. Throws FileNotFoundException, PermissionDeniedException, or IOException if it can't.

methods.name: next
methods.doc: The next record's fields, or null at the end of the file.

methods.name: line
methods.doc: The line the last record read starts on, for messages.
